claims.text: Under ethanol oxidation conditions, catalytic activity is governed by dynamic formation and removal of a sub-monolayer of reactive PGM–oxo species.
Under ethanol oxidation conditions, catalytic selectivity is governed by dynamic formation and removal of a sub-monolayer of reactive PGM–oxo species.
Under ethanol oxidation conditions, catalyst durability is governed by dynamic formation and removal of a sub-monolayer of reactive PGM–oxo species.
The surface oxide/hydroxide layer modulates adsorption energies of key ethanol-oxidation intermediates.
The surface oxide/hydroxide layer facilitates the proton–electron transfer steps needed for complete ethanol oxidation.
Complete oxidation of ethanol involves a 12-electron and 12-proton process.
Controlled pre-oxidation or potential cycling induces a defined sub-monolayer of surface oxo species on PGM nanoparticles.
Oxygen availability and applied potential affect PGM surface speciation during ethanol oxidation.
Formation of a surface oxo layer changes the electronic properties of the catalyst.
Formation of a surface oxo layer lowers activation barriers for ethanol oxidation.
Formation of a surface oxo layer promotes removal of poisoning intermediates.
Partial reduction of the reactive oxide layer after it catalyzes key steps helps maintain long-term durability.
Controlled pre-oxidation that produces sub-monolayer oxo coverage will increase turnover frequency relative to an untreated catalyst.
Controlled pre-oxidation will increase selectivity toward complete ethanol oxidation, producing more CO2 and fewer partial-oxidation products.
The benefit of pre-oxidation will vanish when oxygen availability is too low or the potential window does not permit reformation of the oxide layer.
An oxide layer that becomes too thick blocks active sites.
The proposed mechanism will not operate in extremely reducing environments or when the oxo layer cannot be reformed.
